## When to start dialysis

There is no formal eGFR threshold below which maintenance hemodialysis should begin. Most nephrologists use the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) as a major factor, together with clinical signs and symptoms, the availability of dialysis access, and patient preference [@hemmige2024density]. The IDEAL trial randomized adults with progressive chronic kidney disease to start dialysis at an estimated GFR of 10 to 14 mL/min (early) or 5 to 7 mL/min (late), and found no survival benefit from starting early [@cooper2010ideal]. IDEAL estimated GFR with the Cockcroft-Gault equation, so its thresholds are not exactly CKD-EPI values. After its publication in 2010, the US trend toward earlier initiation levelled off [@li2017trends], and in Canada it reversed [@ferguson2019ideal]; the paper describes it as reversing after 2011 [@hemmige2024density], which is why the cohort here begins in 2011.

## Why facility density

If eGFR alone does not dictate when dialysis starts, the surrounding health system may. The hypothesis of the paper is that areas organized around high-intensity treatment of end-stage disease, with many dialysis facilities per resident, start dialysis earlier than areas oriented toward prevention [@hemmige2024density]. The unit is the Dartmouth Atlas Hospital Service Area (HSA): a group of ZIP codes whose residents get most of their hospital care locally, about 3,400 in the US [@dartmouth_faq]. The paper calls these "health service areas"; this site keeps the abbreviation HSA.

## An open question

Whether the place a patient lives, and the dialysis care around it, affects when dialysis starts is a matter of controversy. The evidence points in more than one direction.

Some studies find that it varies by place more than patients explain. In the United States, mean eGFR at initiation varied between HSAs, and patient characteristics explained only 11% of that variation [@scialla2014iv]; in a later national study, most of the variation in eGFR at initiation, between and within physicians, was not explained by recorded patient or physician characteristics [@li2017trends]. The paper replicated here found that patients in HSAs with the most facilities per resident started at a higher eGFR [@hemmige2024density].

Others find little or no association at a larger scale. In Canada, after adjustment for patients and facilities, none of the explained variation in eGFR at initiation lay between 14 geographic regions, and 3.1% lay between dialysis facilities [@sood2014variation]. Across US states, the number of nephrologists per resident was not associated with mean eGFR at initiation, although it was associated with how many people started dialysis [@ku2015workforce].

The studies do not measure the same thing. Regions and states are far larger than HSAs, Canada has a different health system, and nephrologist supply is not dialysis facility density. An association between an area and its residents found at one scale need not appear at another (see [Area-level exposures](methodological_background.qmd#area-level-exposures)), and part of what looks like an effect of the area may belong to the facility. This replication asks whether the paper's analysis reproduces; it does not settle the controversy.

## The measures

-   **eGFR at initiation** is calculated by the USRDS from the serum creatinine reported on the CMS-2728 Medical Evidence form, using a CKD-EPI equation. The Researcher's Guide describes this variable (`GFR_EPI`) only as calculated with CKD-EPI, and lists a separate variable for the 2021 refit [@usrds2024guide]; `GFR_EPI` is therefore read here as the earlier equation, with the race coefficient [@levey2009ckdepi]. It is kept because it approximates the value physicians saw when deciding. The paper's Methods call it "CKD-EPI equation 2012", the year of the equation that adds cystatin C [@inker2012cystatin]; see the [differences page](differences.qmd#patient-variables).
-   **Facility density** counts the dialysis facilities listed by CMS in the patient's HSA on the date dialysis started, per 100,000 residents [@cms2025dfc].
-   **Area characteristics** come from the American Community Survey [@tidycensus], the USDA rural-urban commuting area codes [@ers2020ruca], and Dartmouth Atlas primary care and hospital measures [@dartmouth_primarycare; @dartmouth_capacity].

## The eGFR thresholds

Three eGFR values, all in mL/min/1.73 m², shape the analysis:

-   **20, the cohort's ceiling.** Patients starting above it are excluded, because the paper restricts to the range nephrologists target for starting dialysis [@hemmige2024density]; earlier work on the same registry used eGFR 5 to 20 as the range commonly targeted for starting [@scialla2014iv]. As in the original code, 20 itself is kept.
-   **10, the definition of an early start.** It is the lower edge of the IDEAL trial's early-start range [@cooper2010ideal], which IDEAL measured on the Cockcroft-Gault scale rather than CKD-EPI. As in the original code, 10 itself counts as early.
-   **5, in one extra analysis.** The original R code also fit the full model only among patients with eGFR above 5. The code does not record why. This analysis is not in the paper.

## Race and eGFR

The race coefficient of the 2009 CKD-EPI equation raises the eGFR of a patient recorded as Black by about 16% for the same creatinine [@levey2009ckdepi]. A Black patient is therefore more likely than another patient with the same creatinine to be counted as starting at an eGFR of 10 or above. Black patients make up a larger share of the patients in denser HSAs (11.3% in HSAs with no facility and 40.6% in the densest, in the paper's Table 1 [@hemmige2024density]). The models adjust for race, and the paper also fits them separately for Black and White patients (eTable 1). Current practice uses the 2021 equation without race [@inker2021ckdepi; @delgado2022unifying]; the replication keeps the paper's measure, because the question is how physicians acted on the eGFR they saw.
